mainTopic: Reading vows by what the person meant: 'until אדר' in a leap year, vows 'until' a holiday, and vows whose purpose limits or cancels them
overview: The גמרא finishes its discussion of a vow 'until ראש חודש אדר.' It brings a ברייתא and shows that, in a leap year, the meaning depends on whether the person knew the year had two אדרs. If he knew, he meant the second אדר; if not, the first. Then a new משנה begins. רבי יהודה and his son רבי יוסי teach that a vow off a food 'until' a holiday ends right when people normally eat that food: wine on פסח night, meat before the fast, garlic on שבת night. The משנה then turns to vows whose purpose is obvious. A vow made to push a friend to accept a gift can be released without a חכם, and רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about a vow demanding that the friend give a gift. Finally, strong-sounding vows made to fend off a marriage or a meal only block the marriage or the meal. The chapter קונם יין then closes with the הדרן.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a vow until ראש חודש אדר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: a vow 'until ראש חודש אדר' lasts until the first אדר, but in a leap year it lasts until the second אדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so too it is taught in a ברייתא: If someone vows 'until ראש חודש אדר,' the vow lasts until ראש חודש of the first אדר. If it was a leap year, it lasts until ראש חודש of the second אדר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up its earlier answer, that unspecified 'אדר' can mean different months depending on the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives two rulings that seem to clash: 'first אדר' and 'second אדר.' This looks like support for splitting the cases. The next steps will figure out exactly how the two halves fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: The first day of a new month
First אדר / second אדר, the two months of אדר in a leap year
A leap year, which has an extra month of אדר

phrases.english: And so it is taught: 'Until the New Moon of אדר'
— the vow lasts until the New Moon of the first אדר;
if it was a leap year —
until the New Moon of the second אדר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer the גמרא gave just before this section, that the meaning of unspecified אדר depends on the case.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that 'אדר' in a vow can mean either the first or the second אדר, depending on the situation
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with two rulings, first אדר and second אדר

steps.title: Is the first part of the ברייתא really not about a leap year?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the second half says 'if it was a leap year,' which seems to mean the first half is not about a leap year. But the first half speaks of a 'first אדר,' which only exists in a leap year.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that the first part is not dealing with a leap year?! (That can't be, because it says 'first אדר.')
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds a problem in how the ברייתא is worded. This sets up the solution in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'First אדר' only exists in a leap year, so the first half must also be talking about a leap year. Then what does the second half's 'if it was a leap year' add? Both halves must be about a leap year, so some other difference must separate them.

keyTerms.meaning: From this it follows; by implication
The first part of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read the second half as 'leap year' versus the first half as 'regular year.' A regular year has no 'first אדר,' so both halves must be about a leap year.

phrases.english: Does this imply that in the first part
we are not dealing with a leap year?!
phrases.notes: This is a surprised question. It can't be a regular year, because a regular year has only one אדר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the ברייתא just quoted and points out a difficulty in its wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of the ברייתא's two halves as regular year versus leap year
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'First אדר' only exists in a leap year, so the first half cannot be about a regular year.

steps.title: The difference is whether he knew it was a leap year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that both halves are about a leap year. If the person knew it was a leap year, he means the second אדר. If he did not know, he means the first אדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this: this case (second אדר) is where he clearly knew the year was a leap year, and that case (first אדר) is where he did not know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the wording problem and confirms its earlier answer: what counts is whether the person knew the year had two אדרs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'If it was a leap year' really means 'if he knew it was a leap year.' Someone who knows about the extra month means the later אדר, while someone unaware means the first one he reaches. This is exactly the split the גמרא suggested before, so the ברייתא supports it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious to him; he clearly knows
The year is made a leap year

steps.whatToRemember: A vow 'until אדר' in a leap year depends on what the person knew: if he knew it was a leap year, it means second אדר; if not, first אדר.

phrases.english: Learn from it:
this case is where it is obvious to him that the year was made a leap year,
phrases.notes: 'This case' is the second half of the ברייתא, the one that says second אדר.

phrases.english: that case is where he did not know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty from the previous step and closes the topic.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both halves of the ברייתא are about a leap year. The difference is whether the person who vowed knew it was a leap year, which supports the גמרא's earlier answer.

steps.title: A wine vow until פסח ends on פסח night
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה teaches that someone who vows off wine 'until it will be פסח' only meant until פסח night, when people normally drink wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: רבי יהודה says: If someone says, 'Wine is קונם, so I will not taste it until it will be פסח,' he only meant until the night of פסח, the time when people usually drink wine.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. רבי יהודה says we read a vow 'until פסח' by what the person most likely meant: the vow stops on פסח night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strictly, 'until פסח' could mean until the end of the holiday. But we assume the person did not want to block himself from the wine people drink on פסח night. So the vow ends right when that drinking time begins.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה; marks the start of a new משנה
A word for making something forbidden by a vow, like a קרבן
The night of פסח, the סדר night

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the main rule of the משנה: a vow 'until' a time is read by what people normally mean, not by the strictest meaning of the words.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Rabbi Yehuda says:
'Wine is konam for me, so I will not taste it
until it will be Passover' —
this person intended nothing
except until the night of Passover,

phrases.aramaic: עַד שָׁעָה שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ בְּנֵי אָדָם לִשְׁתּוֹת יַיִן.
phrases.english: until the time when people usually drink wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה, still about vows that last 'until' a certain time.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow off wine 'until פסח' ends at nightfall of פסח, when people normally drink wine.

steps.title: A meat vow until the fast ends before the fast
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה continues: someone who vows off meat 'until it will be the fast' is only forbidden until the eve of the fast, when people normally eat meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'Meat is קונם, so I will not taste it until it will be the fast,' he is only forbidden until the eve of the fast, because he only meant until the time when people usually eat meat.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a second example of the same rule, this time with meat and the fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People eat a meat meal on the eve of the fast, so we assume he did not mean to block himself from that meal. The vow ends when that meal time comes, before the fast itself starts. This is the same reasoning as the wine case.

keyTerms.meaning: The fast; here it means יום כפור

phrases.english: If he said: 'Meat is konam for me, so I will not taste it
until it will be the fast' —

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ אָסוּר אֶלָּא עַד לֵילֵי צוֹם,
phrases.english: he is forbidden only until the eve of the fast,
because this person intended nothing

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַד שָׁעָה שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ בְּנֵי אָדָם לֶאֱכוֹל בָּשָׂר.
phrases.english: except until the time when people usually eat meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קֻוֽנָּם בָּשָׂר שֶׁאֵינִי טוֹעֵם עַד שֶׁיְּהֵא הַצּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example from רבי יהודה, using the same reasoning as the wine case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow off meat 'until the fast' ends on the eve of the fast, when people normally eat meat.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: a garlic vow until שבת ends on Friday night
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי, son of רבי יהודה, adds that someone who vows off garlic 'until it will be שבת' is only forbidden until שבת night, when people usually eat garlic.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי his son says: If someone says, 'Garlic is קונם, so I will not taste it until it will be שבת,' he is only forbidden until the night of שבת, because he only meant until the time when people usually eat garlic.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי applies his father's rule to a weekly case: a garlic vow 'until שבת' ends when שבת begins on Friday night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה assumes it is common to eat garlic on שבת night. So, just like the wine and meat cases, the vow ends at the time when people normally eat that food.

keyTerms.meaning: The night of שבת, Friday night

steps.whatToRemember: A vow 'until' a holiday or שבת ends when people normally eat that food: wine on פסח night, meat before the fast, garlic on שבת night.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, his son, says:
'Garlic is konam for me, so I will not taste it
until it will be Shabbat,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ אָסוּר אֶלָּא עַד לֵילֵי שַׁבָּת,
phrases.english: he is forbidden only until the night of Shabbat,
because this person intended nothing

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַד שָׁעָה שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ בְּנֵי אָדָם לֶאֱכוֹל בְּשׁוּם.
phrases.english: except until the time when people usually eat garlic.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי יוסי applies his father's rule to garlic and שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow off garlic 'until שבת' ends on שבת night, when people normally eat garlic.

steps.title: A vow meant to make a friend accept a gift
steps.stepSummary: Someone vows not to benefit from his friend unless the friend accepts a gift for his son. The friend can release the vow without a חכם by saying, 'Turning it down is my honor.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone tells his friend, 'Benefit from you is קונם for me unless you come and take a כור of wheat and two barrels of wine for your son,' the friend can undo the vow without a חכם. He just says: 'You only vowed to give me honor. Not taking it is my honor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new topic: vows whose real purpose is obvious. Here a man vows only to push his friend into accepting a gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow was made to honor the friend. So if the friend says 'I feel more honored not taking it,' the vow's goal has been met. The vow falls away without going to a חכם.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make a vow. It makes something forbidden like a קרבן.
Without going to a sage to release it

steps.confusionAlert: 'יכול להפר' here does not mean a husband or father canceling a vow. It means the vow falls away once its purpose is met, when the friend says 'this is my honor,' so no חכם is needed.

phrases.english: One who says to his friend
"It is קונם that I benefit from you
phrases.notes: He means: I am forbidden to get any benefit from you.

phrases.aramaic: אִם אֵין אַתְּ בָּא וְנוֹטֵל לְבָנֶיךָ
phrases.english: if you do not come and take for your son
one כור of wheat
and two barrels of wine"

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי זֶה יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר אֶת נִדְרוֹ
phrases.english: this one can undo his vow
without a sage
And he can say to him:
"Did you say this for any reason other than my honor?
This is my honor."
phrases.notes: He means: not taking the gift is the honor I want.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ קֻוֽנָּם שֶׁאֲנִי נֶהֱנֶה לְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from vows with time limits (steps 4-6) to vows read by their obvious purpose.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow made only to honor someone can be released by that person without a חכם.

steps.title: A vow demanding that a friend give a gift: רבי מאיר's view
steps.stepSummary: Someone forbids his friend from benefiting from him unless the friend gives a gift to his son. רבי מאיר says the friend stays forbidden until he gives it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same goes for someone who tells his friend, 'Benefit from me is קונם for you unless you come and give my son a כור of wheat and two barrels of wine.' רבי מאיר says the friend is forbidden until he gives.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a second case, where the vow pushes the friend to give rather than to take. רבי מאיר gives his ruling first, and the חכמים answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר reads the vow by its plain words: the condition is giving the gift. Until the gift is actually given, the condition has not been met and the friend stays forbidden.

phrases.english: And so too, one who says to his friend
"It is קונם that you benefit from me

phrases.aramaic: אִם אֵין אַתְּ בָּא וְנוֹתֵן לִבְנִי
phrases.english: if you do not come and give my son
a כור of wheat
and two barrels of wine"

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אָסוּר עַד שֶׁיִּתֵּן,
phrases.english: רבי מאיר says: he is forbidden until he gives
phrases.notes: The friend may not benefit from the one who vowed until the gift is handed over.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ קֻוֽנָּם שֶׁאַתְּ נֶהֱנֵית לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips the case from step 7: now the friend must give, not take.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the friend is forbidden until he actually gives the gift.

steps.title: The חכמים: the vower can release it himself
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say that here too the vow can be undone without a חכם. The one who vowed can say, 'I count it as if I received it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: this one too can undo his vow without a חכם. He says to his friend, 'I consider it as though I already received the gift.'
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים argue with רבי מאיר about the case in step 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the חכמים, the gift was meant for the one who vowed, as a kind of honor for him. Since it is his own gain, he can give it up by treating it as already received. The vow then falls away with no need for a חכם.

keyTerms.meaning: As if I had received it

steps.whatToRemember: When a vow is made only to benefit or honor someone, that person can give up the benefit, and the vow falls away without a חכם. רבי מאיר disagrees when the vow demands an actual gift.

phrases.english: And the חכמים say:

phrases.aramaic: אַף זֶה יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר אֶת נִדְרוֹ
phrases.english: even this one can undo his vow
without a sage
and he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Here it is the one who vowed who speaks to his friend.

phrases.english: "I am as though I have received it."

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים אַף זֶה יָכוֹל לְהָפֵר אֶת נִדְרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חכמים: the one who vowed can treat the gift as received, and the vow falls away without a חכם.

steps.title: A vow pushing away a marriage only blocks the marriage
steps.stepSummary: A man pressured to marry his sister's daughter, or a man divorcing his wife, vows that she may never benefit from him. The women may still benefit from him, because he only meant to rule out marriage.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone was pressing a man to marry his sister's daughter, and he said, 'It is קונם that she ever benefits from me,' or a man divorcing his wife said, 'It is קונם that my wife ever benefits from me,' the women may still benefit from him. He only meant to rule out marriage.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two cases where a strong-sounding vow is limited to what the person was really pushing away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'benefits from me forever' sound total. But the setting shows his only goal was to end any talk of marriage. So the vow covers marriage, and every other kind of benefit stays allowed.

phrases.english: If someone was pressing him
to marry his sister's daughter
and he said, "It is קונם that she ever benefits from me"
and likewise one who divorces his wife
and says, "It is קונם that my wife ever benefits from me"
these women are allowed to benefit from him
because this man only meant it
for the sake of marriage

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה מְסָרֵב בּוֹ לָשֵׂאת בַּת אֲחוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another case of reading a vow by its clear purpose, this time to limit it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow said to push away a marriage only forbids the marriage, not other benefit.

steps.title: A vow refusing a meal only blocks the meal
steps.stepSummary: A man pressed to eat at his friend's house vows not to enter or taste even a drop of cold water. He may still enter and drink cold water, because he only meant to refuse a meal.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone was pressing his friend to eat with him, and the friend said, 'It is קונם for me to enter your house, or to taste even a drop of cold water of yours,' he may still enter the house and drink cold water. He only meant to refuse eating and drinking a meal.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more case of a vow that sounds strong but is limited by what the person really meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He used extreme words, 'not even a drop,' only to escape the pressure to stay for a meal. So the vow covers the meal, and entering or drinking a little water stays allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: For the sake of eating and drinking, meaning a meal

steps.whatToRemember: A vow said under pressure is read by what the person was really pushing away, like a marriage or a meal. Strong words do not stretch the vow past that goal.

phrases.english: If he was pressing his friend
to eat with him
and he said, "It is קונם for me to enter your house
or to taste a drop of your cold water"
he is allowed to enter his house
and to drink cold water from him
because this man only meant it
for the sake of eating and drinking

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same idea as step 10, now with a meal instead of a marriage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow said to refuse a meal only forbids the meal, not entering or drinking a little.

steps.title: הדרן: closing the chapter קונם יין
steps.stepSummary: The traditional closing line marks the end of the chapter קונם יין.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'קונם יין'.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new argument or ruling. It is the traditional closing line that says the chapter קונם יין is finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words הדרן עלך mean 'we will return to you.' They express a hope to come back and learn the chapter again. The chapter is named after its opening words, קונם יין.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you': the formula said at the end of every chapter
A word used to make a vow that forbids something, like a קרבן
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא

steps.whatToRemember: The chapter קונם יין ends with a key idea: we read a vow by what the person really meant. Examples are the gift for the son, the niece or wife, and the cold water.
steps.confusionAlert: קונם יין is the name of the chapter, taken from its first words. This line does not rule about a vow on wine.

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'Konam wine'
phrases.notes: 'קונם יין' is the chapter's name, taken from its first words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter right after the last case of the cold water in step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter קונם יין is finished, and the learner promises to return to it.
